But I also think silence about it, including international silence, makes it easier for these incidents to keep happening without consequence. I'm not asking anyone to take my word alone for this. I'm asking people to actually look into it, because the families living through it don't have the platform to make their own case the way international commentary about the 'new Bangladesh' does.

title: Meaning Without a Maker: What I Actually Believe Now
excerpt: After writing so much about what I don't believe, I think it's worth being just as clear about what actually fills that space now, because it isn't nothing.
content:
I've spent a lot of posts explaining the reasons I moved away from religious belief, evidence standards, the problem of evil, institutional failures, personal experience. I think it's worth closing this particular series by being just as direct about what I've built in that space instead, because I don't think the honest answer is emptiness, and I don't want to leave the impression that it is.

Meaning, for me, comes from fairly ordinary sources now: relationships with people I care about, work that feels worth doing, curiosity about how the world actually works, and a sense of responsibility to the people around me that doesn't need a cosmic enforcement mechanism to feel binding. I don't think I treat people well because I'm afraid of consequences in an afterlife, I think I try to treat people well because I can see, directly, how my actions affect them, and that feels like a sufficient reason on its own.

Secular humanism is probably the closest label for where I've landed, a commitment to reason, evidence, and human welfare as the basis for ethics, without needing to ground any of it in the supernatural. I find real intellectual and even something like spiritual satisfaction in things like the scale of the universe, the improbability of conscious life existing at all, the accumulated, hard-won knowledge that got us this far, without needing to attribute any of it to a designer.

I don't think this makes me morally superior to people who believe differently, plenty of religious people live more genuinely ethical lives than I do on any given day. I just think it's important to say clearly that walking away from religious belief wasn't a walk into nothing. For me, it was a walk toward a version of meaning I could actually stand behind without reservations.

title: The Argument From Design, Revisited
excerpt: The old watchmaker analogy, that complexity implies a designer, was one of the first arguments I had to actually sit with and take apart piece by piece.
content:
The watchmaker analogy is one of the oldest arguments in the apologetics toolkit, and it was one of the first ones I ever took seriously enough to actually try to dismantle rather than just accept or reject on instinct. The basic version goes like this: if you found a watch on a beach, you'd assume a watchmaker made it, because its complexity and functional design imply an intelligent creator. Living organisms are far more complex than a watch, so the argument goes, they must imply a far greater designer.

The problem I eventually landed on isn't that the analogy is stupid, it's that it smuggles in an assumption that biological complexity works the same way mechanical complexity does. A watch can't reproduce itself, mutate, or be shaped by differential survival over millions of generations. Evolutionary biology gives a genuinely detailed account of how complex, functional structures can emerge gradually through selection acting on variation, without needing a designer planning the outcome in advance. The eye, often cited as the classic example of irreducible complexity, actually has a well-documented evolutionary pathway through simpler light-sensing structures still visible in living organisms today.

I don't think this fully dissolves every version of the design argument, some contemporary versions focus on the fine-tuning of physical constants rather than biology specifically, and that's a genuinely harder conversation involving cosmology I don't think has a clean settled answer either way. But the classic biological version, once I understood how selection actually works over deep time, stopped carrying the persuasive weight it once had for me.

title: Why I Don't Find Pascal's Wager Convincing
excerpt: Betting on belief because the potential downside of unbelief is infinite sounds clever until you actually try to apply it consistently.
content:
Pascal's Wager gets brought up a lot in these conversations, the idea that believing in God is the rational bet even under uncertainty, because the potential cost of wrongly disbelieving, eternal damnation, vastly outweighs the cost of wrongly believing, a bit of wasted devotion. On its face it has a certain clean, game-theoretic elegance to it.

The problem I kept running into is what philosophers call the many-gods objection, and once I actually thought it through, it broke the wager for me entirely. The argument only works if there are exactly two options on the table, a specific God who rewards belief and punishes disbelief, or no God at all. In reality, there are and have been thousands of different religious traditions throughout history, many making mutually exclusive claims about which specific beliefs and practices are required for salvation and which will be punished. If I "wager" on one tradition's version of God, I'm simultaneously betting against every other tradition's version, some of which might punish exactly the beliefs I'd be adopting to hedge against the first.

There's also something that never sat right with me about the wager as a basis for genuine faith in the first place. It's explicitly a self-interested calculation about hedging cosmic risk, not a claim that the belief is actually true. A God who rewards people for strategically pretending to believe, or for talking themselves into belief purely to avoid punishment, seems like a strange thing to worship even if such a God existed.

I think the wager is clever as a piece of decision theory. I don't think it's a reason to actually believe anything.

title: The Outsider Test: What If I'd Been Born Somewhere Else?
excerpt: The religion most people hold with total conviction is overwhelmingly predicted by where and when they happened to be born. That fact took me a while to really sit with.
content:
One of the ideas that shifted my thinking the most wasn't a knockdown philosophical argument, it was a simple observational fact that's easy to state and surprisingly hard to fully absorb: the specific religion a person holds with total conviction is overwhelmingly predictable from where and when they were born. Someone born in one region grows up certain of one tradition's truth, someone born in another region grows up equally certain of a different, often incompatible tradition's truth, each treating their own upbringing as the one that happened to land on the actual truth of the universe.

Philosophers sometimes call this the outsider test for faith: imagine evaluating your own religion's specific truth claims with the same skeptical distance you'd naturally apply to a religion you weren't raised in. Most people, when encountering an unfamiliar tradition's specific claims, a sacred text found on a hillside, a prophet's visions, a specific set of ritual obligations, apply real scrutiny. That scrutiny tends to relax considerably for the tradition someone happened to be raised inside.

Applying that same outsider scrutiny to the religion I grew up in was uncomfortable, because it meant treating claims I'd been taught to hold as self-evidently true with the same skeptical distance I'd apply to any other tradition's specific claims. Once I actually did that consistently, a lot of what had felt uniquely compelling about my own upbringing started to look more like familiarity than evidence.

I don't think this test proves any specific religion false. I think it's a useful check against mistaking cultural inheritance for independently verified truth, which is a distinction I hadn't taken seriously enough for a long time.

title: Facing Mortality Without an Afterlife
excerpt: Losing the promise of an afterlife is, for a lot of people, the hardest part of walking away from belief. I don't think I've fully resolved it, but I've found something workable.
content:
I won't pretend this is the easy part. Of everything I've had to work through, the loss of a promised afterlife is the one that still visits me at inconvenient moments, usually late at night, usually after thinking about someone I've lost or will eventually lose. There's a specific kind of comfort in believing that death isn't really an ending, and losing access to that comfort honestly, rather than just intellectually, took longer than any of the philosophical arguments did.

What I've settled into, and I want to be honest that "settled" is doing some optimistic work in that sentence, is less a triumphant answer and more a shift in what I focus on. If this life is what I actually have, rather than a waiting room for something else, then the specific relationships, moments, and work that fill it matter more, not less, because there isn't a cosmic do-over where I get to make different choices. That reframe doesn't erase the fear, but it does something useful with it.

I also think there's an honesty in facing mortality without a promised continuation that I've come to value, even on the hard days. I'm not managing my life around securing a specific outcome in a place I can't verify exists. I'm trying to build something meaningful with the actual, finite time I know I have, and there's a clarity in that which I don't think I had access to before.

I don't think I've conquered the fear of death. I don't think most people, believers included, ever fully do. But I've found a way to hold it that feels honest rather than borrowed, and that matters to me.

title: Raising Kids Without Religion: What I Actually Tell Them
excerpt: Not handing children a religious framework doesn't mean handing them nothing. It means being more deliberate about where their sense of meaning and morality actually comes from.
content:
One question I get asked more than almost any other, usually by people who mean it genuinely rather than as a gotcha, is what I actually tell my kids instead of religion. I understand the question, because a lot of religious upbringing does real work: explaining death, providing a moral framework, offering a sense of belonging and ritual. Simply subtracting religion without replacing any of that would leave a real gap.

What I've tried to do instead is be more deliberate, not less, about each of those pieces individually. On death, I try to be honest rather than either falsely reassuring or needlessly bleak, acknowledging it's sad and permanent while focusing on how the people we lose live on in memory and impact. On morality, I try to ground it in empathy and consequences I can actually explain, how does this action affect another person, rather than in an appeal to divine command or fear of punishment. On belonging, we've found that through extended family, community groups, and just consistent, intentional time together, rather than through a weekly religious service specifically.

I also try not to raise them as the mirror image of a religious upbringing, teaching them that non-belief is the obviously correct position everyone smart eventually reaches. I want them to actually understand why people believe what they believe, and to be capable of forming their own conclusions once they're old enough to genuinely wrestle with these questions themselves, rather than just inheriting my answer as an unquestioned replacement for someone else's unquestioned answer.

It's more work than handing them a ready-made framework would be. I think it's also more honest, and so far, it feels like the right tradeoff.

title: Building Community Outside of Mashjid
excerpt: Losing my faith meant losing a ready-made community too, and I underestimated how much work it would take to rebuild that part deliberately.
content:
Nobody warned me how much the community side of this would matter. I'd expected to wrestle with the philosophical questions, the arguments about evidence and suffering and design. What I hadn't fully anticipated was how much of my actual social infrastructure, people I saw weekly, a built-in support network during hard times, a sense of belonging to something larger than myself, was tied directly to a religious institution I was stepping away from.

Rebuilding that has genuinely been the harder, slower project. Secular community spaces exist, but they don't have the same centuries of institutional momentum behind them, the automatic weekly gathering, the built-in rituals for marking birth, marriage, and death, the assumption that showing up will connect you with people. I had to be a lot more intentional about finding and maintaining community than I'd ever needed to be when a religious institution was doing a lot of that structural work for me by default.

What's worked for me has been a combination of things, none as complete on its own as the community I left behind: closer, more deliberate friendships that I actively maintain rather than assume will sustain themselves, volunteer work that provides both purpose and regular social contact, and secular or humanist gathering groups that, while smaller and less established, do exist and are growing in a lot of places.

I don't think I've fully replaced what I lost, and I'm honest with myself about that. But I've come to see community-building as something I now have to actively practice rather than passively inherit, and there's been an unexpected value in that too, even on the days it feels like more effort than it used to require.

title: Four Years of Writing This Blog, and I'm Still Not Done
excerpt: Looking back on everything this country and this party have been through since I started keeping this record, and why I'm still here writing about it.
content:
When I started writing on this blog, none of what's happened since would have seemed plausible to me. A bridge opening, a metro running, an economy holding steady through a global crisis, and then, within a couple of years, a government toppled, a party banned, friends and family scattered or silenced. It's been a strange four years to live through, let alone write about honestly.

I've tried, in these posts, to hold two things at once: real pride in what got built during those years, and real grief over how it all came apart and what's happened to people I care about since. I know plenty of readers will think I'm biased, and they're right, I am, I've never pretended otherwise on this blog. But bias isn't the same thing as dishonesty, and I've tried hard not to lie about what I've seen, even when the truth was uncomfortable for my own side.

I don't know what the next few years hold for this party or this country. Elections may or may not happen on the timeline anyone's promising. But I know I'm not going to stop writing about it, because I think the people who lived through this deserve more than one version of the story, and this has always been mine.

title: Where Morality Actually Comes From, If Not From God
excerpt: The question I get asked most often, in one form or another, is how I can have a coherent sense of right and wrong without a divine lawgiver behind it.
content:
The question comes up in a lot of different phrasings, but it boils down to the same thing: without God as the source of moral law, what stops morality from just being arbitrary personal preference? I understand why the question feels urgent to people who've always had morality anchored to something outside themselves. I don't think the anchor it needs has to be supernatural, though.

The version of secular ethics I find most compelling grounds morality in something fairly concrete: the actual, observable effects our actions have on the wellbeing of other conscious beings capable of suffering and flourishing. That's not arbitrary in the way "just personal preference" implies, it's testable and reasoned about the same way other empirical claims are, even if it doesn't have the certainty of a divine command. We can argue about specific applications, and people do, but the underlying commitment, that suffering matters and flourishing matters, doesn't require a supernatural source to function as a real, binding framework.

I'd also push back gently on the assumption that divine command actually solves the arbitrariness problem rather than just relocating it. If something is good only because a deity commands it, that starts to look arbitrary in its own way, dependent entirely on that particular deity's will rather than on any deeper reasoning about why it's actually good. Philosophers have been arguing about this exact tension, sometimes called the Euthyphro dilemma, for over two thousand years, and I don't think divine command ethics resolves it as cleanly as it's often presented.

I don't think secular ethics is easier than religious ethics. I think it just puts the hard work of moral reasoning in a different, and to me more honest, place.

title: The Comfort of Prayer, and Why I Miss It Sometimes
excerpt: I don't think prayer works the way I once believed it did, but I'll admit I still miss the specific kind of comfort it used to provide, and I think that honesty matters.
content:
I want to write something a little more vulnerable than usual, because I think a lot of writing from an atheist perspective leans hard into the intellectual case and skips past something I still feel, even years into this: I miss praying. Not because I think it worked the way I once believed, sending a request outward to be heard and possibly answered, but because it gave me a specific, structured space to sit with fear, gratitude, and uncertainty that I haven't fully replaced.

What I've come to understand is that prayer was probably doing something real, just not the something I thought it was doing at the time. The act of articulating a worry out loud, sitting with it in stillness, naming what I was grateful for, that has genuine psychological value regardless of whether anything on the other end was listening. It's closer to a structured meditation or an act of self-reflection than a genuine two-way communication, but the value of that structure was real even if my explanation for why it worked was wrong.

I've tried to rebuild something like that, quiet, deliberate reflection, sometimes written down, sometimes just sitting with a difficult feeling instead of rushing past it, without the theological framing attached. It's not identical, and I won't pretend it fully replaces what prayer gave me, particularly in genuinely frightening moments where the old habit of reaching out to something bigger than myself still surfaces almost automatically.

I think it's worth admitting that walking away from belief doesn't mean every part of the old framework was worthless. Some of it was doing real psychological work, and I think the honest move is to keep what actually helped, even after discarding the explanation that used to justify it.

title: Coming Out as an Atheist to My Family
excerpt: Telling the people closest to me that I no longer shared their faith was, in some ways, harder than any of the philosophical arguments I'd already worked through.
content:
Working through the arguments, evidence, the problem of evil, textual criticism, was, in a strange way, the easier part of this whole process. Telling my own family was harder, because it wasn't an intellectual exercise anymore, it was a conversation that risked changing how people who loved me saw me, and how comfortable they felt around me.

I put it off for longer than I probably should have, partly out of fear of disappointing people, partly out of a genuine reluctance to cause them pain over something I knew mattered enormously to them. When I finally did have the conversation, it went about as well as these things reasonably can, which is to say it wasn't smooth, there was real hurt and real worry on their end, questions about whether I still had values at all, whether this reflected something they'd failed to instill.

What helped, over time, wasn't winning any argument. It was continuing to show up as the same person I'd always been, someone who still cared about them, still showed up for family obligations, still lived according to values they could recognize even if the framework underneath had changed. I think a lot of the initial fear on their side wasn't really about the specific philosophical position, it was about whether losing the shared belief meant losing the shared relationship too.

I don't think every family reconciles as gracefully as mine eventually did, and I don't want to pretend this conversation is easy or safe for everyone in every family or community. But for anyone facing that same conversation, I'd say the relationship usually survives better than the fear anticipates, provided both sides are willing to keep showing up for each other through the disagreement.

title: Holidays and Traditions I Keep, Just Without the Theology
excerpt: I still gather with family for the holidays I grew up celebrating. What's changed is what I understand myself to be actually celebrating when I do.
content:
I still put up decorations for the holidays I grew up with. I still gather with extended family for the same seasonal celebrations that shaped my childhood. What's different is what I actually understand myself to be marking when I do, and I think that distinction matters more to me than it probably looks like from the outside.

A lot of religious holidays sit on top of much older seasonal and agricultural traditions anyway, marking solstices, harvests, and the turning of the year long before any specific theology attached itself to those dates. I find real value in leaning into that older layer, the natural rhythm of the year, the gathering of people who matter to me at meaningful points in the calendar, the specific family recipes and rituals that have nothing to do with doctrine and everything to do with shared history.

I've had to be honest with family members about the shift, some holidays involve specific religious observances I no longer participate in with genuine belief, and I try to be respectful about that rather than either performing belief I don't have or making a point of visibly opting out in a way that turns a family gathering into a statement. Mostly that's meant quietly stepping back from specific religious components while staying fully present for the parts that are really about togetherness.

I don't think keeping these traditions makes me inconsistent. I think it reflects something I've come to believe more broadly: that a lot of what religion provided, ritual, seasonal rhythm, connection to people I love, doesn't actually require the theology underneath it to still be worth keeping.

title: Two Years Later: Has Bangladesh Found the Stability It Was Promised?
excerpt: It's been two years since the interim government took over promising reform and stability. I think it's fair to ask honestly whether that promise has been kept.
content:
Two years ago, we were told this transition would fix everything that was supposedly broken. But I look around Dhaka today, and I can't help asking: what exactly needed fixing? The last seventeen years under the Awami League were, on balance, the best this country has seen — and we're now watching nearly every gain from that era be squandered, one by one.

Under the Awami League, Bangladesh was one of the fastest-growing economies in the world. The taka was stable, foreign reserves were healthy, and millions of people were lifted out of poverty. Today the currency is under constant pressure and ordinary families feel the squeeze at every market and every petrol pump. The economic managers of the last seventeen years had their flaws like any government, but they understood something fundamental: stability and continuity are what allow a country to prosper. We've traded that for chaos.

Law and order is another story that doesn't get told honestly. Under the Awami League government, people could open their shops without fear, travel at night, and do business without looking over their shoulders. Now the complaints from ordinary shopkeepers and small business owners — the kind of people who rarely speak up publicly about politics — have gotten louder, not quieter. That silence breaking should worry anyone paying attention.

And then there are the elections. The Awami League delivered election after election, on time, with real campaigns and real choices. Elections that were supposed to happen under this interim arrangement have been delayed and delayed again, with shifting justifications each time — all while those who won at the ballot box are sidelined and vilified. Meanwhile, the infrastructure projects that were moving forward under the last government — the metro rail, the expressways, the power plants, the bridges — the very projects that made me write with real pride a few years back, have slowed to a crawl or stalled entirely.

I'm not claiming the last seventeen years were perfect — no government anywhere is. But judged on its own terms — growth, stability, infrastructure, women's empowerment, food security — the Awami League record stands up against any in our history. After two years, it's time to stop grading this interim period against the mistakes of the past and start asking what it has actually delivered. From where I sit, that answer isn't a comfortable one for the people currently in charge.

I still believe this country did better, on balance, with the Awami League government that could be held accountable at the ballot box than with the current arrangement. I hope we get the chance to test that belief again soon, at an actual election, where the people — not the streets, not the hashtags — get to decide.
